source_refs.note: Practice MCQs written from Chapter 2 (PDF 22-45, printed 22-45); not printed in the book. Based on the chapter's text, tables, boxes and worked examples (numericals with changed values); none repeats the chapter exercise. Drafts needing academic review.

blocks.text: Practice MCQs for the whole of Chapter 2 (Atomic Structure), arranged by the chapter's sections. Each question has one correct answer with a short explanation; numerical questions show the working.
2.1 Atomic number, proton number and nucleon number; identity of an element

blocks.prompt: 1 Moseley found that the square root of the frequency of the characteristic X-rays of an element is directly proportional to its:
blocks.explanation: Moseley (1913): √ν ∝ Z, the atomic number (2.1).

book_ref.quote: the square root of the frequency of the X-rays was directly proportional to the atomic number

blocks.prompt: 2 In Moseley's experiment, characteristic X-rays were produced when different elements were bombarded with:
blocks.explanation: Elements bombarded with cathode rays gave X-rays of characteristic frequencies (2.1).

book_ref.quote: when different elements were bombarded with cathode rays

blocks.prompt: 3 The atomic number of an element is also called its:
blocks.explanation: Atomic number Z is a fundamental property of an element and is also called proton number (2.1).

book_ref.quote: It is also called proton number.

blocks.prompt: 4 The nucleon number (A) of an atom is the:

options.text: total number of protons and neutrons in its nucleus
total number of protons and electrons

blocks.explanation: The number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus together is the nucleon number (A), also called mass number (2.1).

book_ref.quote: collectively called its nucleon number (A), also called mass number

blocks.prompt: 5 Which equation correctly relates mass number (A), atomic number (Z) and number of neutrons (N)?
blocks.explanation: A = Z + N, so N = A − Z (2.1).

book_ref.quote: Atomic number is related to the mass number by the following equation

blocks.prompt: 6 How many neutrons are present in an atom of ⁴⁰₂₀Ca?

book_ref.quote: Number of neutrons in an atom can be calculated as

blocks.prompt: 7 An atom of ⁴⁰₂₀Ca loses two electrons to form Ca²⁺. The number of electrons in Ca²⁺ is:
blocks.explanation: Electrons = 20 − 2 = 18; protons (20) and neutrons (20) do not change (2.1).

book_ref.quote: atom loses three electrons to form Al³⁺

blocks.prompt: 8 ¹⁹₉F gains one electron to form F⁻. The numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in F⁻ are respectively:
blocks.explanation: Protons = 9; neutrons = 19 − 9 = 10; electrons = 9 + 1 = 10 (2.1).

book_ref.quote: gains an electron to form Cl⁻ ion

blocks.prompt: 9 The number of electrons in the ion ⁵⁶₂₆Fe³⁺ is:
blocks.explanation: Electrons = 26 − 3 = 23 (30 is the number of neutrons, 56 − 26) (2.1).

book_ref.quote: atom loses three electrons to form Al³⁺

blocks.prompt: 10 ¹⁴₇N gains three electrons to form N³⁻. How many electrons does N³⁻ have?
blocks.explanation: Electrons = 7 + 3 = 10 (2.1).

book_ref.quote: In case electron gain happens by the neutral atoms

blocks.prompt: 11 According to Table 2.1, which two ions have the same number of electrons and the same number of neutrons?
blocks.explanation: S²⁻ and P³⁻ both have 18 electrons and 16 neutrons, though protons differ (16 and 15) (2.1).

book_ref.quote: Table 2.1 Number of protons, electrons and neutrons in different ions

blocks.prompt: 12 When a neutral atom forms an ion, which numbers stay the same?
blocks.explanation: Ion formation only adds or removes electrons; e.g. Al → Al³⁺ keeps 13 protons and 14 neutrons (2.1).

book_ref.quote: the number of electrons, protons, and neutrons can be justified for an ion

blocks.text: 2.2 Effect of an electric field on the fundamental particles

blocks.prompt: 13 The behaviour of a beam of fundamental particles in an electric field depends upon their:
blocks.explanation: Behaviour in an electric field depends upon mass and charge (2.2).

book_ref.quote: The behaviour of particles in an electric field depends upon their mass and charge.

blocks.prompt: 14 A beam of neutrons passing through an electric field:

options.text: is not deflected and travels in a straight path

blocks.explanation: Neutrons are neutral, so they are not deflected (2.2).

book_ref.quote: Neutrons being neutral are not deflected but travel in a straight path

blocks.prompt: 15 In an electric field, protons are deflected towards the:
blocks.explanation: Protons are positively charged, so they bend towards the negative plate (2.2).

book_ref.quote: Protons being positively charged are deflected towards the negative plate.

blocks.prompt: 16 Electrons are deflected to a greater extent than protons in an electric field because electrons are:

options.text: faster than protons at the same speed

blocks.explanation: Their charges are equal in size, but the electron is 1/1836 of the proton's mass (2.2).

book_ref.quote: to greater extent since they are 1/1836 times lighter than protons

blocks.prompt: 17 The angle of deflection of a particle in an electric field is proportional to:
blocks.explanation: Angle of deflection ∝ charge/mass (2.2).

book_ref.quote: The amount of deviation from its original direction of movement is measured in two ways.

blocks.prompt: 18 The radius of deflection of a charged particle is proportional to:
blocks.explanation: Radius of deflection ∝ mass/charge, the reciprocal of the factor for the angle (2.2).

book_ref.quote: the factors affecting the radius of deflection are reciprocal to that for the angle of deflection

blocks.prompt: 19 An electron and a proton enter the same electric field at the same speed. Which one has the larger radius of deflection?
blocks.explanation: Radius ∝ mass/charge; the charges are equal in size and the proton is heavier, so its radius is larger (2.2).

book_ref.quote: after deflection, the particle moves in a circular path

blocks.prompt: 20 According to Table 2.2, the charge on a proton is:
blocks.explanation: Proton: charge +1.6022 × 10⁻¹⁹ coulomb, relative charge +1 (2.2.1).

book_ref.quote: Table 2.2 Properties of three fundamental particles

blocks.prompt: 21 The mass of an electron given in Table 2.2 is:
blocks.explanation: Electron mass = 9.1095 × 10⁻³¹ kg = 5.4858 × 10⁻⁴ amu (2.2.1).

book_ref.quote: Table 2.2 Properties of three fundamental particles

blocks.prompt: 22 Which of the three fundamental particles has the largest mass?
blocks.explanation: Neutron 1.0087 amu > proton 1.0073 amu > electron 5.4858 × 10⁻⁴ amu (2.2.1).

book_ref.quote: shows the properties of three fundamental particles electron, proton and neutron

blocks.prompt: 23 Using the masses in kg from Table 2.2, the ratio (mass of proton)/(mass of electron) is closest to:

book_ref.quote: Table 2.2 Properties of three fundamental particles

blocks.prompt: 24 Using Table 2.2, the charge-to-mass ratio (e/m) of the electron is about:

book_ref.quote: Table 2.2 Properties of three fundamental particles

blocks.prompt: 25 By how many amu is the neutron heavier than the proton (Table 2.2)?

book_ref.quote: Table 2.2 Properties of three fundamental particles

blocks.text: 2.3 Experimental evidence for the electronic configuration

blocks.prompt: 26 The modern theory of electronic structure originates from:

options.text: the Bohr model of the atom

blocks.explanation: The modern theory of electronic structure originates from the Bohr model (2.3).

book_ref.quote: The modern theory of electronic structure originates from the Bohr Model of atom.

blocks.prompt: 27 The two main sources of experimental evidence for electronic configuration are:
blocks.explanation: Evidence derives principally from atomic spectra and ionization energies (2.3).

book_ref.quote: derives principally from two sources; atomic spectra and ionization energies

blocks.prompt: 28 A gaseous element is subjected to electrical discharge. The spectrum of the radiation it gives out is a(n):

options.text: atomic absorption spectrum of dark lines
atomic emission spectrum of coloured lines
spectrum with no lines at all

blocks.explanation: Heating or electrical discharge makes the gas emit certain wavelengths: coloured lines, the atomic emission spectrum (2.4.1).

book_ref.quote: The spectrum of this radiation contains coloured lines and is called atomic emission spectrum.

blocks.prompt: 29 In an atomic absorption spectrum, the absorbed wavelengths appear as:

options.text: coloured lines on a dark background

blocks.explanation: Wavelengths absorbed from white light show up as dark lines (2.4.1).

book_ref.quote: show up as dark lines on the spectrum

blocks.prompt: 30 To obtain an atomic absorption spectrum, white light is passed through a gaseous sample of the element that is:
blocks.explanation: Absorption: white light through the gaseous element in the cold state (2.4.1).

book_ref.quote: passed through a gaseous sample of an element in cold state

blocks.prompt: 31 Compared with the coloured lines of the emission spectrum of the same element, the dark lines of its absorption spectrum have:
blocks.explanation: The dark lines are at exactly the same wavelengths as the coloured lines (2.4.1).

book_ref.quote: The wavelengths of the dark lines in the absorption spectrum are exactly the same as those of coloured lines

blocks.prompt: 32 Atomic spectra are called the finger prints of the elements because:

options.text: each element has a unique set of fixed energy levels and so its own characteristic spectrum
all elements give the same lines

blocks.explanation: Unique electron arrangement → unique energy levels → unique wavelengths, so each element is identified by its spectrum (2.4.1).

book_ref.quote: atomic spectra are the finger prints of the elements

blocks.prompt: 33 Which of the following is the wavelength of one of the visible lines of the hydrogen spectrum?
blocks.explanation: The visible hydrogen lines are at 410, 434, 486 and 656 nm (2.4.1, corrected figure).

book_ref.quote: The visible hydrogen lines are at 410, 434, 486 and 656 nm

blocks.text: 2.3.2 Relation between ionization energy and energy levels (electronic shells)

blocks.prompt: 34 Ionization energies are used to investigate electronic configurations by studying:

options.text: only the mass numbers of elements
the radius of deflection of electrons
successive ionization energies of one element and first ionization energies of different elements

blocks.explanation: The two ways: successive IEs of the same element, and first IEs of different elements (2.3.2).

book_ref.quote: Ionization energies are used to investigate the electronic configurations of elements in two ways.

blocks.prompt: 35 The second ionization energy, ΔHᵢ₂, of an element X refers to the change:
blocks.explanation: ΔHᵢ₁: X → X⁺ + e⁻; ΔHᵢ₂: X⁺ → X²⁺ + e⁻ (2.3.2).

book_ref.quote: We call this sequence of ionization energies, successive ionization energies.

blocks.prompt: 36 As electrons are removed one by one from an atom, the successive ionization energies:

options.text: first increase and then fall to zero

blocks.explanation: Successive IEs increase from the valence shell to the inner shells (2.3.2).

book_ref.quote: successive ionization energies increase when we move from the valence shell to the inner shells

blocks.prompt: 37 In the successive ionization energies of magnesium, the first large increase occurs on removing the:
blocks.explanation: Two outer electrons come off easily; the third must come from a shell much closer to the nucleus (2.3.2).

book_ref.quote: But, a large increase occurs when the third electron is removed.

blocks.prompt: 38 From the successive ionization energies of magnesium, how many electrons are shown to be in its second shell?
blocks.explanation: Electrons 3 to 10 (the third, then seven more) come from the second shell: 8 electrons (2.3.2).

book_ref.quote: The next seven electrons are removed successively from the second shell

blocks.prompt: 39 For magnesium, the most enormous jump in ionization energy occurs when the following electron is removed:
blocks.explanation: The 11th and 12th electrons come from the innermost shell, right next to the nucleus (2.3.2).

book_ref.quote: A similar but much more enormous jump occurs when the eleventh and twelfth electrons are removed.

blocks.prompt: 40 The two large jumps in the successive ionization energies of magnesium show that its electrons are in:
blocks.explanation: Two large jumps separate three groups of electrons: three shells (2.3.2).

book_ref.quote: These two large jumps in the series of successive ionization energies are very good evidence

blocks.prompt: 41 All ionization energies are:
blocks.explanation: It takes energy to separate an electron from an atom, so ionization is strongly endothermic (2.3.2).

book_ref.quote: All ionization energies are strongly endothermic

blocks.prompt: 42 First ionization energy decreases down a group because:

options.text: the number of shells increases and the nucleus holds the valence electrons less strongly
electrons are added to the same shell

blocks.explanation: Down the group shells increase, the hold of the nucleus on valence electrons decreases (2.3.2).

book_ref.quote: down the group, number of shells increases, hold of nucleus on the valence electrons decreases

blocks.prompt: 43 Ionization energy generally increases across a period because:

options.text: electrons are added to the same shell while the proton number increases
the valence electrons are farther from the nucleus

blocks.explanation: Across a period the shell number stays the same while protons increase, so the nucleus attracts valence electrons more (2.3.2).

book_ref.quote: As the proton number increases, electrons are added in the same shell.

blocks.prompt: 44 Within each period, the highest first ionization energy belongs to:
blocks.explanation: Alkali metals have the lowest and noble gases the highest IE in each period (2.3.2).

book_ref.quote: The group 1 elements, the alkali metals, have the lowest ionization energy within each period

blocks.prompt: 45 Which of the following has the highest first ionization energy?
blocks.explanation: Noble gases are highest in their periods and IE falls down the group He → Ne → Ar; so helium is highest (2.3.2).

book_ref.quote: from helium to neon to argon, or from lithium to sodium to potassium

blocks.prompt: 46 The first large jump in the successive ionization energies of an element comes between ΔHᵢ₁ and ΔHᵢ₂. The number of electrons in its outermost shell is:
blocks.explanation: Only one electron is removed before the jump to an inner shell, so the valence shell has 1 electron (2.3.2).

book_ref.quote: The successive ionization energies show clearly the arrangement of electrons in shells

blocks.prompt: 47 The Bohr model described the distribution of electrons using:
blocks.explanation: Bohr's one-dimensional model used only n, for the size and energy of the orbit (2.5).

book_ref.quote: The Bohr model was a one-dimensional model that used one quantum number

blocks.prompt: 48 Schrödinger's model needs three quantum numbers to describe orbitals because:
blocks.explanation: A 3-D space needs three coordinates, i.e. three quantum numbers n, ℓ and m (2.5).

book_ref.quote: it required three coordinates, or three quantum numbers

blocks.prompt: 49 The three quantum numbers n, ℓ and m together describe an orbital's:

options.text: size, shape and orientation in space

blocks.explanation: n, ℓ and m describe the size, shape and orientation of orbitals (2.5).

book_ref.quote: These quantum numbers describe the size, shape, and orientation in space of the orbitals in an atom.

blocks.prompt: 50 The principal quantum number n describes the:

options.text: size and energy of the orbital

blocks.explanation: n describes size and energy; ℓ the shape; m the orientation (2.5.1).

book_ref.quote: This quantum number, n, describes the size and energy of the orbital.

blocks.prompt: 51 The shell with principal quantum number n = 3 is designated by the letter:
blocks.explanation: n = 1, 2, 3, 4 … are designated K, L, M, N … (2.5.1).

book_ref.quote: The principal quantum number, n, can have positive integral values 1,2,3,4

blocks.prompt: 52 The collection of orbitals with the same value of n is called a(n):
blocks.explanation: Same n → electron shell; same n and ℓ → subshell (2.5.1).

book_ref.quote: The collection of orbitals with the same values of n is called an electron shell.

blocks.prompt: 53 As n increases, an electron in the orbital:

options.text: has higher energy and is less tightly bound to the nucleus
has lower energy and is more tightly bound

blocks.explanation: Larger n: greater average distance, larger orbital, higher energy, less tightly bound (2.5.1).

book_ref.quote: the electron has a higher energy and is therefore less tightly bound to the nucleus

blocks.prompt: 54 Using the formula 2n², the maximum number of electrons in the shell with n = 5 is:

book_ref.quote: maximum number of electrons in a shell by the formula 2n²

blocks.prompt: 55 The maximum numbers of electrons that the K, L, M and N shells can accommodate are respectively:

book_ref.quote: Therefore shells K, L, M and N can accommodate maximum electrons.

blocks.prompt: 56 For a given value of n, the azimuthal quantum number ℓ can have values:
blocks.explanation: ℓ takes integral values 0 to (n − 1) (2.5.2).

book_ref.quote: can have integral values 0 to (n- 1) for each value of n

blocks.prompt: 57 The azimuthal (angular momentum) quantum number describes the orbital's:
blocks.explanation: ℓ describes the shape of the orbital (2.5.2).

book_ref.quote: This quantum number describes the shape of the orbital.

blocks.prompt: 58 For n = 3, the possible values of ℓ are:

book_ref.quote: If n=3 there are, three values of

blocks.prompt: 59 The letters s, p, d and f used for ℓ values stand for:
blocks.explanation: These are spectral terms: sharp, principal, diffused, fundamental (2.5.2).

book_ref.quote: which stand for sharp, principal, diffused and fundamental, respectively

blocks.prompt: 60 A subshell is a set of orbitals having the same values of:
blocks.explanation: Same n and ℓ → subshell (2.5.2).

book_ref.quote: The set of orbitals that have the same n and ℓ values is called a subshell.

blocks.prompt: 61 Using 2(2ℓ + 1), the maximum number of electrons in a subshell with ℓ = 2 is:

book_ref.quote: The number of electrons in a subshell can be calculated by the formula 2(2ℓ+1)

blocks.prompt: 62 How many subshells are present in the N shell (n = 4)?
blocks.explanation: The number of subshells equals the shell number: 4s, 4p, 4d, 4f (2.5.2).

book_ref.quote: The number of subshells in a shell is equal to its shell number.

blocks.prompt: 63 Which of the following subshells does not exist?
blocks.explanation: For n = 2, ℓ can only be 0 or 1 (2s, 2p); ℓ = 2 (d) needs n ≥ 3 (2.5.2).

book_ref.quote: Table 2.4 Relationship between n, ℓ and subshells

blocks.prompt: 64 According to Table 2.3, the shape of an orbital with ℓ = 2 is:
blocks.explanation: ℓ = 0 spherical, 1 dumbbell, 2 cloverleaf (double dumbbell), 3 complicated (2.5.2).

book_ref.quote: Table 2.3 Shapes of orbital

blocks.prompt: 65 An electron is in a subshell with n = 4 and ℓ = 3. The subshell is:
blocks.explanation: ℓ = 3 is designated f, so n = 4, ℓ = 3 is 4f (2.5.2).

book_ref.quote: Similarly, if n=4, there are four values of

blocks.prompt: 66 For a given value of ℓ, the number of possible values of m is:
blocks.explanation: m runs from −ℓ through 0 to +ℓ: (2ℓ + 1) values (2.5.3).

book_ref.quote: For a certain value of ℓ there are (2ℓ + 1) integral values of m

blocks.prompt: 67 For ℓ = 2, the values of the magnetic quantum number m are:
blocks.explanation: −ℓ … 0 … +ℓ gives −2, −1, 0, +1, +2: five d orbitals (2.5.3).

book_ref.quote: there are five values of m, namely

blocks.prompt: 68 How many orbitals are there in an f subshell?
blocks.explanation: ℓ = 3 gives seven m values (−3 to +3): 7 orbitals; 14 is the number of electrons (2.5.3).

book_ref.quote: It means f-subshells have 7 orbitals.

blocks.prompt: 69 Degenerate orbitals are orbitals that:

options.text: belong to the same subshell and have the same energy

blocks.explanation: Orbitals of the same subshell have the same energy: degenerate orbitals (2.5.3).

book_ref.quote: Orbitals of the same subshell have same energy and are called degenerate orbitals.

blocks.prompt: 70 Degenerate orbitals are differentiated from each other in the presence of a(n):
blocks.explanation: Their differentiation in a magnetic field gives m the name magnetic quantum number (2.5.3).

book_ref.quote: differentiated from each other in the presences of magnetic field

blocks.prompt: 71 The presence of orbitals in subshells is indicated by:

options.text: deflection of neutrons in an electric field
splitting of fine spectral lines in a magnetic field

blocks.explanation: Splitting of fine lines in a magnetic field indicates orbitals in subshells (2.5.3).

book_ref.quote: Splitting of small fine lines in the presence of magnetic field

blocks.prompt: 72 An orbital has m = −3. The smallest possible value of ℓ for this orbital is:
blocks.explanation: m ranges from −ℓ to +ℓ, so m = −3 needs ℓ ≥ 3 (an f orbital) (2.5.3).

book_ref.quote: The values of m indicate the number of orbitals in a subshell.

blocks.prompt: 73 According to electromagnetic theory, an electron behaves like a magnet because:

options.text: a spinning charge generates a magnetic field
it is heavier than a proton
it moves in a straight line

blocks.explanation: The electron spins about its own axis; a spinning charge generates a magnetic field (spin quantum number).

book_ref.quote: a spinning charge generates a magnetic field

blocks.prompt: 74 The possible values of the spin quantum number s are:
blocks.explanation: s = +½ or −½, for the two possible spinning motions (spin quantum number).

book_ref.quote: it is necessary to introduce a fourth quantum number

blocks.prompt: 75 The clockwise spin of an electron (s = +½) is represented by:
blocks.explanation: Clockwise, s = +½: up arrow ↑; anticlockwise, s = −½: down arrow ↓ (corrected text).

book_ref.quote: The clockwise spin (s = +½) is represented by an arrow (↑) pointing upwards

blocks.prompt: 76 An orbital can accommodate at the most:

options.text: two electrons with the same spin

blocks.explanation: Each orbital holds at most two electrons, provided their spins are opposite (spin quantum number).

book_ref.quote: Each orbital can accommodate at the most two electrons

blocks.prompt: 77 The fourth quantum number is needed in order to:

options.text: describe the size of an orbital
differentiate between the two electrons in the same orbital
describe the shape of an orbital
describe the orientation of an orbital

blocks.explanation: Three quantum numbers describe an orbital; the fourth (s) differentiates its two electrons (spin quantum number).

book_ref.quote: fourth quantum number to differentiate between the two electrons

blocks.prompt: 78 The total number of orbitals in the shell with n = 4 is:
blocks.explanation: n² = 4² = 16 orbitals (1 + 3 + 5 + 7); 32 is the number of electrons (spin quantum number box).

book_ref.quote: there are n subshells consisting of n² orbitals

blocks.prompt: 79 An atomic orbital is the three-dimensional region around the nucleus where:

options.text: the probability of finding the electron is maximum
the electron moves in a fixed circular orbit

blocks.explanation: Definition of an atomic orbital (2.6).

book_ref.quote: the probability of finding the electron is maximum

blocks.prompt: 80 In an s orbital, the electron density around the nucleus is:
blocks.explanation: An s orbital is spherical with uniform electron density in all directions (2.6.1).

book_ref.quote: The electronic density around the nucleus in an s orbital is uniformly distributed in all directions.

blocks.prompt: 81 Compared with the 1s orbital, the 2s orbital is:
blocks.explanation: s orbitals are spherical and grow larger as n increases (2.6.1).

book_ref.quote: With the increase in the principal quantum number, the size of s orbital also becomes larger.

blocks.prompt: 82 The electron density of a 2p orbital, unlike that of an s orbital:

options.text: forms a doughnut in the xy plane only

blocks.explanation: A p orbital is not spherically symmetric; its density lies in lobes along an axis (2.6.2).

book_ref.quote: The electron density is not distributed in a spherically symmetric fashion

blocks.prompt: 83 The three p orbitals are named px, py and pz according to:

options.text: the axes along which they lie
the number of electrons in them

blocks.explanation: Each p orbital is named after its axis (2.6.2).

book_ref.quote: The p orbitals are named as px, py, and pz accordingly to their axes.

blocks.prompt: 84 The dxz orbital lies in the:
blocks.explanation: dxy, dxz and dyz lie in the xy, xz and yz planes respectively (2.6.3).

book_ref.quote: The dxy, dxz, and dyz lie in the xy, xz, and yz planes, respectively.

blocks.prompt: 85 Which d orbital has its lobes lying along the x and y axes?
blocks.explanation: The lobes of dx²−y² lie along the x and y axes; dxy lies between them in the xy plane (2.6.3).

book_ref.quote: lie along the x and y axes

blocks.prompt: 86 The d orbital with two lobes along the z-axis and a doughnut in the xy plane is:
blocks.explanation: The dz² orbital has two lobes along z and a doughnut in the xy plane (2.6.3).

book_ref.quote: orbital has two lobes along the z-axis

blocks.prompt: 87 Which statement about f orbitals is given in the chapter?

options.text: there are five f orbitals shaped like cloverleaves
there are seven f orbitals and their shapes are very complicated
there are three dumbbell-shaped f orbitals

blocks.explanation: An f subshell has seven orientations (seven f orbitals); their shapes are very complicated (2.6.3).

book_ref.quote: An f subshell has seven orientations in space

blocks.prompt: 88 Electronic configuration is the:

options.text: distribution of electrons among the shells, subshells or orbitals of an atom or ion
number of protons in the nucleus
arrangement of neutrons in the nucleus

blocks.explanation: Definition of electronic configuration (2.7).

book_ref.quote: Electronic configuration is the distribution of electrons among available shells, subshells, or orbitals

blocks.prompt: 89 In the notation 2p⁵, the superscript 5 gives the:

options.text: number of electrons in the 2p subshell

blocks.explanation: The superscript on a subshell symbol gives the number of electrons in that subshell (2.7).

book_ref.quote: This gives the number of electrons in the subshell.

blocks.prompt: 90 In an orbital diagram, an arrow pointing downward represents an electron with:
blocks.explanation: Up arrow: s = +½; down arrow: s = −½ (2.7).

book_ref.quote: The arrow points upward, when s = +

blocks.prompt: 91 The L shell can hold a maximum of 8 electrons, in its:
blocks.explanation: L shell (n = 2): 2s and 2p, 8 electrons maximum (2.7.1).

book_ref.quote: L shell (n=2): 8 electrons maximum (2s and 2p orbitals)

blocks.prompt: 92 The electrons of a sodium atom occupy the:

options.text: K, L, M and N shells

blocks.explanation: Na: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹ uses the K, L and M shells (2.7.1).

book_ref.quote: Sodium (Na): 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹ (K, L, and M shells)

blocks.prompt: 93 The M shell (n = 3) contains which orbitals?
blocks.explanation: M shell: 3s, 3p and 3d, holding 18 electrons maximum (2.7.1).

book_ref.quote: M shell (n=3): 18 electrons maximum (3s, 3p, and 3d orbitals)

blocks.text: 2.7.2 Distribution of electrons in subshells and orbitals: the Aufbau principle

blocks.prompt: 94 The Aufbau principle is also known as the:
blocks.explanation: Aufbau = building up principle (2.7.2).

book_ref.quote: Aufbau principle is also known as the building up principle.

blocks.prompt: 95 According to the Aufbau principle, subshells are filled with electrons in:

options.text: alphabetical order s, p, d, f only

blocks.explanation: Subshells fill in increasing order of energy (2.7.2).

book_ref.quote: the subshells in an atom are filled with electrons in an increasing order of their energy values

blocks.prompt: 96 In the absence of a magnetic field, the energy of a subshell depends upon:
blocks.explanation: Energy depends on n and ℓ, so the filling order comes from (n + ℓ) (2.7.2).

book_ref.quote: depends upon the principal quantum number (n) and the azimuthal quantum number

blocks.prompt: 97 The (n + ℓ) value of the 5p subshell is:

book_ref.quote: The subshell having lower (n + ℓ) value has lower energy and is filled first.

blocks.prompt: 98 Which subshell is filled first: 5s or 4d?

options.text: 5s, because its (n + ℓ) = 5 is lower than 6 for 4d
both fill at the same time

blocks.explanation: 5s: 5 + 0 = 5; 4d: 4 + 2 = 6; lower (n + ℓ) fills first (2.7.2).

book_ref.quote: The subshell having lower (n + ℓ) value has lower energy and is filled first.

blocks.prompt: 99 The 4f and 5d subshells both have (n + ℓ) = 7. Which is filled first?

options.text: 4f, because it has the lower n
5d, because it has the lower ℓ
5d, because it has the higher n
both fill at exactly the same time

blocks.explanation: With equal (n + ℓ), the subshell with lower n is filled first: 4f before 5d (2.7.2).

book_ref.quote: then the subshell with lower

blocks.prompt: 100 Which energy order of subshells is correct according to the (n + ℓ) rule?

book_ref.quote: According to this rule the energy wise arrangement of orbitals should be.

blocks.prompt: 101 Among 3d, 4p and 5s, which all have (n + ℓ) = 5, the subshell filled last is:
blocks.explanation: Equal (n + ℓ): lower n first, so 3d → 4p → 5s (2.7.2).

book_ref.quote: Table 2.6 (n + ℓ) values of various sub-shells.

blocks.text: Pauli's exclusion principle (printed as a second 2.7.2)

blocks.prompt: 102 Pauli's exclusion principle states that no two electrons in an atom can have:

options.text: the same values for all four quantum numbers

blocks.explanation: No two electrons in an atom can have all four quantum numbers the same (Pauli's principle).

book_ref.quote: No two electrons in an atom can have the same values for all the four quantum numbers

blocks.prompt: 103 The two electrons of a helium atom differ only in their:
blocks.explanation: Both have n = 1, ℓ = 0, m = 0; one has s = +½ and the other s = −½ (Pauli's principle).

book_ref.quote: In the first shell of helium (He) atom, there are two electrons.

blocks.prompt: 104 The set of quantum numbers (n, ℓ, m, s) for the second electron of a helium atom is:
blocks.explanation: Second 1s electron: n = 1, ℓ = 0, m = 0, s = −½ (Table of the two He electrons).

book_ref.quote: It means that their spins are in the opposite directions.

blocks.prompt: 105 Hund's rule is about filling electrons into:
blocks.explanation: Hund's rule deals with orbitals having equal energies, e.g. px, py, pz (2.7.4).

book_ref.quote: This rule gives an idea for filling electrons into the orbitals having equal energies.

blocks.prompt: 106 Three electrons are placed in the three 2p orbitals. According to Hund's rule they are arranged:

options.text: two in px and one in py
one in each orbital, all with the same spin
one in each orbital, with alternate spins

blocks.explanation: Degenerate orbitals are singly occupied first, with the same spin (2.7.4).

book_ref.quote: the correct way of filling three electrons in three p orbitals is that in which each orbital is singly occupied

blocks.prompt: 107 How many unpaired electrons are present in a ground-state oxygen atom (1s² 2s² 2p⁴)?
blocks.explanation: 2p⁴: one orbital is paired, two orbitals each have one electron → 2 unpaired (2.7.4, Fig. 2.14).

book_ref.quote: they should be placed in separate orbitals with the same spin

blocks.prompt: 108 In an electrons-in-boxes diagram, the boxes are arranged in order of:

options.text: decreasing energy from bottom to top
increasing energy from bottom to top

blocks.explanation: Each box is an orbital; boxes go up in increasing energy (2.7.5).

book_ref.quote: The boxes (orbitals) can be arranged in order of increasing energy from bottom to top.

blocks.prompt: 109 Electrons occupy separate orbitals of the same subshell wherever possible in order to:
blocks.explanation: Electrons in the same region repel each other (same charge); separate orbitals minimize repulsion (2.7.5).

book_ref.quote: electrons will occupy separate orbitals in the same subshell to minimize this repulsion

blocks.prompt: 110 How many unpaired electrons does a carbon atom (1s² 2s² 2p²) have in the ground state?
blocks.explanation: The two 2p electrons go into separate p orbitals with the same spin → 2 unpaired (2.7.5, Fig. 2.14).

book_ref.quote: Electrons are only paired when there are no more empty orbitals available within a subshell.

blocks.prompt: 111 According to Table 2.7, the ground-state configuration of chromium (Z = 24) is:
blocks.explanation: Table 2.7: Cr is 3d⁵4s¹ (3d⁵4s² is Mn) (2.7.5).

book_ref.quote: Electronic configuration of ground states of elements

blocks.prompt: 112 According to Table 2.7, the configuration of copper (Z = 29) ends in:
blocks.explanation: Cu: …3d¹⁰4s¹; Zn: …3d¹⁰4s²; Ni: …3d⁸4s² (2.7.5).

book_ref.quote: Electronic configuration of ground states of elements

blocks.prompt: 113 An element has the configuration 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶3d¹⁰4s²4p³. Its atomic number is:

book_ref.quote: Electronic configuration of ground states of elements

blocks.text: 2.8 Electronic configuration and the periodic table

blocks.prompt: 114 The outer configuration of group 2 elements is:
blocks.explanation: Group 1: ns¹; group 2: ns²; group 13: ns²np¹ (2.8).

book_ref.quote: the group 1 and 2 elements all have ns¹ and ns² outer configurations respectively

blocks.prompt: 115 Elements of group 13 have the outer configuration:
blocks.explanation: Group 13: ns²np¹ (2.8).

book_ref.quote: When we jump to group 13 elements, we find that they have ns²np¹ configuration.

blocks.prompt: 116 The block of ten columns in the middle of the periodic table contains elements in which:
blocks.explanation: Ten columns = transition metals, d orbitals filling; d holds 10 electrons (2.8).

book_ref.quote: In the middle of the table is a block of ten columns that contain the transition metals.

blocks.prompt: 117 The number of columns in the p-block on the right of the periodic table is:
blocks.explanation: Six columns, because a p subshell holds 6 electrons (2.8).

book_ref.quote: On the right is a block of six columns.

blocks.prompt: 118 The two rows below the main table, containing fourteen columns, are the:
blocks.explanation: The f-block: f orbitals are being filled; f holds 14 electrons (2.8).

book_ref.quote: Below the main portion of the table are two rows that contain fourteen columns.

blocks.prompt: 119 How many valence electrons does phosphorus (1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p³) have?
blocks.explanation: Outermost shell n = 3: 3s² 3p³ → 5 valence electrons (2.8.1).

book_ref.quote: The electrons in an atom in the outermost shell are called valence electrons.

blocks.prompt: 120 Elements in the same group have similar chemical properties because they have similar:
blocks.explanation: Valence electrons take part in reactions; similar valence configurations give similar properties (2.8.1).

book_ref.quote: The similarities among the configurations of valence electrons account for similarities of the chemical properties

blocks.text: 2.8.2 Classification of the elements of the periodic table

blocks.prompt: 121 The valence-shell configuration of all representative (main-group) elements has the form:
blocks.explanation: Representative elements: nsᵃ npᵇ; the outer s or p subshell is being filled (2.8.2).

book_ref.quote: The main-group or representative elements all have valence-shell configurations

blocks.prompt: 122 In the inner-transition elements, the subshell being filled is:
blocks.explanation: Inner-transition (f-block): an f subshell is being filled (2.8.2).

book_ref.quote: In the f-block transition elements or inner-transition elements

blocks.prompt: 123 In the d-block (yellow) area of Figure 2.16, the subshell being filled is:
blocks.explanation: Blue: ns; green: np; yellow: (n − 1)d; light golden: (n − 2)f (2.8.2).

book_ref.quote: In the yellow area, an (n

blocks.prompt: 124 The order in which subshells are filled across the fourth period is:
blocks.explanation: Fourth period: 4s, then 3d, then 4p (2.8.2).

book_ref.quote: We start building-up order by starting with the first period

blocks.prompt: 125 The division of elements into blocks s, p, d and f is done on the basis of their:
blocks.explanation: Classification is based on electronic configuration and valence electrons (2.8.2).

book_ref.quote: This division is done on the basis of electronic configuration and their valence electrons.

blocks.prompt: 126 The ion Mg²⁺ (proton number 12) has the same electronic configuration as:
blocks.explanation: Mg²⁺ has 12 − 2 = 10 electrons: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶, like neon (as for Na⁺ in 2.9.1).

book_ref.quote: Note that this is the same as the electronic configuration of neon

blocks.prompt: 127 Which of the following ions has the same electronic configuration as argon?
blocks.explanation: Cl⁻ has 17 + 1 = 18 electrons, like argon; Na⁺, Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ have 10 (2.9.1).

book_ref.quote: which is the same as argon, the element with 18 electrons in each atom

blocks.prompt: 128 When an atom of a d-block element of period 4 forms a positive ion, electrons are lost first from the:
blocks.explanation: 4s fills before 3d, but 4s electrons are lost first when ions form (2.9.1).

book_ref.quote: when atoms of a d-block element lose electrons to form ions, the 4s electrons are lost first

blocks.prompt: 129 Using the configuration of Fe in Table 2.7 (…3d⁶4s²), the configuration of Fe²⁺ is:
blocks.explanation: The two 4s electrons are lost first: Fe²⁺ = …3d⁶ (2.9.1).

book_ref.quote: Reading across the Periodic Table from potassium to zinc

blocks.prompt: 130 How many 3d electrons are present in Cr³⁺?
blocks.explanation: Cr: 3d⁵4s¹. Losing the 4s electron and two 3d electrons leaves 3d³ (2.9.1).

book_ref.quote: Cr³⁺ ion: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d³

blocks.prompt: 131 A free radical is a species that has:
blocks.explanation: Definition of a free radical (2.9.2).

book_ref.quote: A free radical is a species that has one or more unpaired electrons

blocks.prompt: 132 In the chlorine free radical Cl• (1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁵), the unpaired electron is in the:
blocks.explanation: 2p⁶ is full; in 3p⁵ two orbitals are paired and one has a single electron (2.9.2, corrected).

book_ref.quote: In the 3p subshell, two orbitals have paired electrons whereas the third one contains a single unpaired electron.

blocks.prompt: 133 Which of the following is a free radical formed by a group of atoms?
blocks.explanation: Groups of atoms such as OH• and CH₃• can be free radicals (2.9.2).

book_ref.quote: Apart from single atoms, groups of atoms can also be free radicals.

blocks.prompt: 134 In the symbol of a free radical, such as Cl•, the unpaired electron is shown by:
blocks.explanation: The unpaired electron is shown by a single dot (2.9.2).

book_ref.quote: The unpaired electron is shown by a single dot

blocks.text: 2.10 Electronic configuration and the formation of semiconductors

blocks.prompt: 135 Semiconductors are materials that:

options.text: conduct only in the liquid state
can conduct electricity under some conditions

blocks.explanation: Semiconductors conduct electricity under some conditions (2.10).

book_ref.quote: Semiconductors are materials that can conduct electricity under some conditions.

blocks.prompt: 136 In a pure silicon crystal (₁₄Si = 2, 8, 4), each Si atom is bonded to:
blocks.explanation: Si has 4 valence electrons; in the pure crystal each Si is bonded to four other Si atoms (2.10).

book_ref.quote: In the pure crystalline form, each Si atom is bonded to four other Si atoms.

blocks.prompt: 137 Electronic conduction through a pure silicon crystal is:
blocks.explanation: In pure crystalline Si all four valence electrons are bonded, so there is no electronic conduction (2.10).

book_ref.quote: there is no possibility of electronic conduction through the Si crystal

blocks.prompt: 138 Doping pure silicon with boron produces a(n):

options.text: pure conductor with no charge carriers

blocks.explanation: Trivalent impurities (B, Al) create P-type; pentavalent (P, As) create N-type (2.10).

book_ref.quote: adding trivalent impurities (like boron or aluminum) creates a P-type semiconductor

blocks.prompt: 139 Which impurity, added to pure silicon, creates an N-type semiconductor?
blocks.explanation: Pentavalent impurities such as phosphorus or arsenic give N-type (2.10).

book_ref.quote: adding pentavalent impurities (like phosphorus or arsenic) creates an N-type semiconductor

blocks.prompt: 140 The main charge carriers in a P-type semiconductor are:
blocks.explanation: P-type: holes (positive carriers); N-type: extra electrons (negative carriers) (2.10).

book_ref.quote: The difference lies in whether the added impurity creates

blocks.prompt: 141 When aluminium atoms take the place of some Si atoms in a silicon crystal, the semiconductor formed is:

options.text: P-type, with holes as positive charge carriers

blocks.explanation: Al has three valence electrons, so holes form: a positive-type, i.e. P-type, semiconductor (corrected 2.11.1).

book_ref.quote: A positive-type semiconductor is a P-type semiconductor, not an N-type one.

blocks.prompt: 142 Holes are created in the crystal lattice of P-type silicon because:

options.text: each Si atom gains an extra electron
the impurity has five valence electrons
the silicon atoms cannot make four bonds due to the lack of electrons

blocks.explanation: Trivalent atoms supply one electron too few, so Si cannot make four bonds and holes form (2.11.1).

book_ref.quote: The silicon atoms cannot make four bonds due to the lack of electrons.

blocks.prompt: 143 In N-type silicon doped with phosphorus, the charge carriers are:

options.text: the extra (fifth) electrons of phosphorus, free to move

blocks.explanation: Four of P's five valence electrons form bonds; the fifth is extra and free to move as a negative carrier (2.11.2).

book_ref.quote: the fifth electron is an extra electron

blocks.prompt: 144 The number of valence electrons of the impurity atoms used to make an N-type semiconductor is:
blocks.explanation: N-type uses pentavalent impurity (5 valence electrons); P-type uses trivalent (3) (2.11.2).

book_ref.quote: When impurity atoms with five valence electrons (like phosphorus) are added
